children.title: Units & Measurement
Why do we need agreed units at all?
children.summary: Measures a table in spans, cubits and feet and gets three different numbers. 'Large' or 'small' means nothing without a standard

children.title: Why are SI units now defined by constants of nature?
children.summary: Watches an artefact kilogram drift while c, h and the caesium frequency stay fixed. The metre is defined through c

children.title: Why only seven base units?
children.summary: Builds newtons, joules and watts from kg, m and s in a derived-unit builder

children.title: Why is a radian dimensionless, and what is a steradian?
children.summary: Sees arc ÷ radius and area ÷ r² cancel their units

children.title: Why do we bother with significant figures?
children.summary: Writes 2.308 cm as 0.02308 m and 23.08 mm: the number of reliable digits stays at four whatever the unit

children.title: Why do products keep the fewest sig figs but sums the fewest decimals?
children.summary: Multiplies and adds measurements with error bars and sees which rule protects the precision

children.title: Why does 2.745 round to 2.74 but 2.735 to 2.74?
children.summary: Rounds many numbers both ways and sees that 'round half to even' cancels the upward bias

children.title: Why do relative errors add when you multiply?
children.summary: Multiplies 16.2 ± 0.1 cm by 10.1 ± 0.1 cm and gets ± 1.6% as the area's error strips

children.title: Significant-figure drill
children.summary: Counts sig figs and rounds correctly

children.title: Orders of magnitude: atom to Earth
children.summary: Places the hydrogen atom (10⁻¹⁰ m) and Earth (10⁷ m) 17 orders apart on a powers-of-ten ladder

children.title: Measure a hair or a thread with simple tools
children.summary: Winds a thread round a pencil, or uses a microscope, to beat a ruler's least count

children.title: Dimensions
Why can't you add a velocity to a force?
children.summary: Treats units as algebra and sees only like dimensions survive a '+'

children.title: Why doesn't 'dimensionally correct' mean 'correct'?
children.summary: Sees ½mv² and (3/16)mv² both pass the dimension check, though only one is true

children.title: Why must sin, log and eˣ take pure numbers?
children.summary: Tries sin(5 m) and finds it meaningless, then sees that angles are ratios

children.title: Why doesn't a pendulum's period depend on its mass?
children.summary: Solves T = k lˣ gʸ mᶻ by matching dimensions; the mass exponent is forced to 0 (spec below)
children.spec: Guess: T = k lˣ gʸ mᶻ, with sliders for x, y and z. Dimensions: the [L], [T] and [M] exponents are shown live, and only x = ½, y = −½, z = 0 balance. Check: a virtual pendulum with changeable mass and length confirms it, and k is measured as about 2π. Limit: dimensional analysis can't give k. A label says so.

children.title: Dimensional-formula builder
children.summary: Assembles [M L T] exponents for any quantity

children.title: Convert units between systems
children.summary: Rewrites a calorie or G in new mass, length and time units

children.title: Where does c go in m = m₀/√(1 − v²)?
children.summary: Fixes a half-remembered formula by making the bracket dimensionless

children.title: Motion in a Straight Line
Why is 'velocity at an instant' a limit?
children.summary: Shrinks Δt from 2 s to 0.01 s for x = 0.08t³; Δx/Δt settles at 3.84 m/s at t = 4 s

children.title: Why is velocity a slope and displacement an area?
children.summary: Reads the slope of x–t and the area under v–t, and checks the axes' units to see why an area can be a distance

children.title: How can something be at rest yet accelerating?
children.summary: Throws a ball up: at the top v = 0 but a = −g

children.title: Why doesn't the sign of a say speeding up or slowing down?
children.summary: Flips the axis direction and compares a with v instead

children.title: Why is average speed ≥ |average velocity|?
children.summary: Walks to a closed market and back: the average velocity is 0, but the walker is tired

children.title: Why must real motion graphs be smooth?
children.summary: Zooms into a kink and sees an infinite acceleration nature can't supply

children.title: Linked x–t, v–t, a–t graphs
children.summary: Drags one graph and the other two follow

children.title: Which graph can't be real motion?
children.summary: Rejects impossible graphs such as two positions at once or negative time

children.title: Uniform Acceleration
Why do the three equations of motion come from one picture?
children.summary: Reads the area of the trapezium under a straight v–t line to get x = v₀t + ½at², then v² = v₀² + 2ax (spec below)
children.spec: Graph: a straight v–t line from v₀ with slope a. Area: rectangle v₀t plus triangle ½at² equals the displacement x. Eliminate t: substituting t = (v − v₀)/a turns the area into v² = v₀² + 2ax. Check: a live cart on a track matches all three equations.

children.title: Why do the equations fail when a changes?
children.summary: Lets a vary with time and watches the formula drift from the true motion; the calculus version still works

children.title: Galileo's odd numbers: why falls go 1 : 3 : 5 : 7
children.summary: Drops a ball and marks equal time intervals

children.title: Why does doubling speed quadruple stopping distance?
children.summary: Brakes at 11, 15, 20 and 25 m/s and finds the distance goes as v₀²

children.title: Which equation do I use?
children.summary: Ticks the known quantities and gets the right equation

children.title: Relative velocity on a line
children.summary: Rides with one train and watches the other

children.title: Measure your reaction time with a ruler
children.summary: Catches a dropped ruler: 21 cm means about 0.21 s

children.title: One equation for the whole flight
children.summary: Throws a ball up from a 25 m roof; a single quadratic gives the 5 s landing

children.title: Vectors
Why do vectors need the triangle law?
children.summary: Adds a 3 m walk and a 4 m walk at different angles: the result ranges from 1 m to 7 m

children.title: Why is displacement ≤ path length?
children.summary: Takes many routes between the same two points

children.title: Why do components make adding easy?
children.summary: Splits vectors into x and y parts and adds each column separately

children.title: Why is the resultant formula the law of cosines?
children.summary: Sees R² = A² + B² + 2AB cos θ: the angle between the vectors is the supplement of the triangle's angle

children.title: Component calculator
children.summary: Uses Aₓ = A cos θ and A_y = A sin θ, and back

children.title: Where to hold the umbrella
children.summary: Adds rain at 35 m/s and wind at 12 m/s and tilts the umbrella 19° from vertical

children.title: Boat in a current
children.summary: Combines a 25 km/h boat with a 10 km/h current

children.title: Projectiles
Why can horizontal and vertical motion be treated separately?
children.summary: Drops one ball and throws another sideways at the same instant; they land together (spec below)
children.spec: Twin drop: one ball dropped, one thrown sideways at the same moment, with strobe images every 0.1 s. Rows line up: the heights match at every flash, and the horizontal gaps stay equal. Shadows: the x-shadow moves uniformly and the y-shadow falls like free fall. Combine: x = v cos θ t and y = v sin θ t − ½gt² give the parabola.

children.title: Why is a projectile's path a parabola?
children.summary: Eliminates t and finds y = (tan θ)x − kx²

children.title: Why does 45° give the longest range?
children.summary: Sweeps θ and sees R ∝ sin 2θ peak at 2θ = 90°

children.title: Why do 45° ± α give equal ranges? (Galileo)
children.summary: Overlays the two paths and sees sin(90° ± 2α) is the same

children.title: Why is velocity always tangent to the path?
children.summary: Shrinks the chord Δr until it lies along the tangent

children.title: Same gravity, straight line or parabola?
children.summary: Changes only the launch velocity: initial conditions shape the path

children.title: Projectile calculator
children.summary: Gives the time of flight, maximum height and range

children.title: A cricket throw at 28 m/s, 30°
children.summary: Reaches 10 m high and lands 69 m away

children.title: A stone thrown off a 490 m cliff
children.summary: Lands after 10 s at about 99 m/s

children.title: Circular Motion
Why is there acceleration at constant speed?
children.summary: Draws the Δv triangle around the circle; it always points to the centre

children.title: Why is a = v²/R?
children.summary: Sees the position triangle and the velocity triangle are similar

children.title: Why is v = ωR?
children.summary: Turns the same angle on a bigger circle and covers more arc

children.title: Why don't the equations of motion work in circles?
children.summary: Sees |a| stay constant while its direction keeps turning

children.title: ω, v, T and ν converter
children.summary: Converts between the four circular-motion quantities

children.title: Aircraft loop: how many g?
children.summary: Flies a 1 km loop at 900 km/h: a ≈ 6.4 g

children.title: Insect in a groove
children.summary: Makes 7 revolutions in 100 s: ω ≈ 0.44 rad/s
